claims.sentence: The thyroid is a gland in the neck that makes hormones which help control the body's energy use.
claims.evidence: Search excerpt: thyroid is a small gland in the front of the neck that makes T4 and T3; thyroid hormones control how the body uses energy.

claims.sentence: When it makes too little hormone the body's processes slow down, and when it makes too much they speed up.
claims.evidence: No retrieved NHS text states slowing down/speeding up of body processes; NHS pages only say too little / too much hormone.
claims.newSentence: An underactive thyroid does not make enough of these hormones, while an overactive thyroid makes too much.

claims.sentence: The NHS describes an underactive thyroid as a common condition in which the thyroid does not make enough hormone.
claims.evidence: NHS: underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism) is a common condition where the thyroid gland in your neck does not make enough hormones.

claims.sentence: Typical symptoms are tiredness, feeling cold, weight gain, constipation, low mood, and dry skin or hair loss.
claims.evidence: NHS lists tiredness, feeling colder than usual, weight gain, constipation, low mood, dry skin or hair, hoarse voice. 'Hair loss' not stated.
claims.newSentence: Common symptoms include tiredness, feeling colder than usual, weight gain, constipation, low mood, and dry skin or hair.

claims.sentence: Symptoms may be mild and can develop slowly, so they are not always easy to notice.
claims.evidence: NHS: symptoms can be mild and easy to miss; usually develop slowly and get worse over time.

claims.sentence: The NHS says an overactive thyroid, also called hyperthyroidism, means the thyroid makes too much hormone.
claims.evidence: NHS overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism) page: Graves' disease makes the thyroid overproduce hormone; treatments aim to stop excess hormone. Title pairs overactive with hyperthyroidism.

claims.sentence: Symptoms include nervousness or irritability, difficulty sleeping, persistent tiredness, sensitivity to heat, and a fast or irregular heartbeat.
claims.evidence: NHS lists nervousness, anxiety, mood swings, sleep problems, tiredness, heat sensitivity, fast or irregular heartbeat, tremors, weight loss. 'Irritability' and 'persistent' not stated.
claims.newSentence: Symptoms can include nervousness, anxiety, mood swings, sleep problems, tiredness, sensitivity to heat, and a fast or irregular heartbeat.

claims.sentence: Weight loss despite a normal or increased appetite and a swelling in the neck, called a goitre, can also occur.
claims.evidence: Weight loss and tremors listed by NHS; appetite detail and goitre as a symptom not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Tremors and weight loss can also occur, and it is unlikely that one person would have all of the symptoms.

claims.sentence: In the UK, the main cause of an underactive thyroid is Hashimoto's disease, an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the thyroid.
claims.evidence: NHS: in the UK the main cause is Hashimoto's disease, an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks the thyroid.

claims.sentence: The main cause of an overactive thyroid is Graves' disease, another autoimmune condition.
claims.evidence: NHS: Graves' disease is an autoimmune condition; about 4 in 5 people with an overactive thyroid have it (NHS 111 Wales says about 3 in 4).

claims.sentence: Thyroid nodules and some medicines can also cause it.
claims.evidence: NHS 111 Wales: nodules can cause an overactive thyroid, less commonly. Medicines as a cause of overactive thyroid not retrieved (medicines are a cause of underactive thyroid per NHS).
claims.newSentence: Thyroid nodules can also cause an overactive thyroid, though less commonly.

claims.sentence: An underactive thyroid is usually treated with levothyroxine tablets, which replace the missing hormone.
claims.evidence: NHS: treatment is usually levothyroxine tablets taken daily; replaces hormone the thyroid does not make.

claims.sentence: The NHS says they are usually needed for life, with regular blood tests to check that the treatment is right.
claims.evidence: NHS: usually take levothyroxine for the rest of your life; regular blood tests check the dose.

claims.sentence: An overactive thyroid can be treated with antithyroid medicine, radioactive iodine or surgery.
claims.evidence: NHS treatment page: antithyroid medicine, radioactive iodine, surgery.

claims.sentence: Beta blockers can ease symptoms such as palpitations in the meantime.
claims.evidence: Retrieved text: beta blockers help control some symptoms while overactivity is brought under control; they do not stop over-production. Palpitations not named.
claims.newSentence: Beta blockers can help control some of the symptoms in the meantime, but they do not stop the thyroid making too much hormone.

claims.sentence: Radioactive iodine often leads to an underactive thyroid that then needs lifelong hormone tablets.
claims.evidence: Treatment pages: main side effect of radioactive iodine is an underactive thyroid; if thyroid is underactive or removed you take medicine for life.

claims.sentence: Thyroid function is checked with blood tests that measure thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and thyroid hormones.
claims.evidence: NHS diagnosis: blood tests measuring TSH and thyroxine (T4); high TSH with low T4 may mean underactive, low TSH with high T3/T4 usually overactive.

claims.sentence: The site's pages on thyroid function tests and TSH explain them, and the laboratory report shows the reference range used.
claims.evidence: Meta pointer to site pages; reference ranges vary between laboratories (retrieved), harmless.

claims.sentence: A GP appointment is the route for symptoms that could be thyroid-related.
claims.evidence: NHS says a GP may examine the neck and order blood tests; the 'route for symptoms' wording is not stated.
claims.newSentence: A GP can examine your neck and arrange blood tests to check how well the thyroid is working.

claims.sentence: The NHS advises calling 999 if a thyroid storm, a rare and life-threatening flare-up of an overactive thyroid, is suspected.
claims.evidence: NHS complications page: thyroid storm is rare, life-threatening, a medical emergency, can follow undiagnosed or poorly controlled overactive thyroid. No retrieved text names 999.
claims.newSentence: Thyroid storm is a rare, life-threatening flare-up of an overactive thyroid that the NHS calls a medical emergency, so it needs a 999 call.

claims.sentence: An underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism) means the gland does not make enough thyroid hormone; an overactive one (hyperthyroidism) means it makes too much.
claims.evidence: As c03 and c06.

claims.sentence: Symptoms are broadly opposite: tiredness and feeling cold with an underactive thyroid, weight loss and feeling hot with an overactive one.
claims.evidence: 'Broadly opposite' not stated; tiredness appears in both lists.
claims.newSentence: Symptoms differ: an underactive thyroid can cause tiredness, feeling cold and weight gain, while an overactive one can cause nervousness, sensitivity to heat, a fast heartbeat and weight loss.

claims.sentence: The main cause of an underactive thyroid in the UK is an autoimmune condition called Hashimoto's disease.
claims.evidence: As c09.

claims.sentence: Underactive thyroid is usually treated with levothyroxine tablets; overactive thyroid with medicine, radioactive iodine or surgery.
claims.evidence: As c12 and c14.

claims.sentence: Treatment for an overactive thyroid can lead to an underactive thyroid, so follow-up blood tests matter.
claims.evidence: NHS lists treatment for an overactive thyroid as a cause of underactive thyroid; regular blood tests monitor hormone levels.

claims.sentence: An underactive thyroid makes too little hormone and slows the body down; an overactive thyroid makes too much and speeds it up.
claims.evidence: As c02: slowing/speeding not stated in retrieved text.
claims.newSentence: An underactive thyroid does not make enough thyroid hormone, while an overactive thyroid makes too much; the symptoms, causes and treatments differ.

notes: Graves' share: NHS main page via search summary says about 4 in 5; NHS 111 Wales says about 3 in 4, so no figure is used. 999 for thyroid storm was not found in any retrieved NHS text; the edited sentence relies on general emergency practice and should be spot-checked on the NHS complications page. Hashimoto's causes and 'about' figures were from search summaries, not full pages.
